lessons.culture: Banks in Iraq usually open in the morning and close in the early afternoon, and the weekend is Friday and Saturday, so plan your visit for Sunday to Thursday. Bring your ID (الهوية) to open an account. Amounts are quoted in thousands of dinars, the dollar is often used alongside the dinar, and exchange offices are common.

lessons.culture: At the post office the clerk weighs a parcel at the counter and the price follows the weight and the country. Addresses in Iraq are often given by district, street and a nearby landmark, so write the landmark and a phone number on a parcel. For anything urgent many people use a private courier company instead.

lessons.culture: In Iraq most people use prepaid lines and top up with a scratch card or an app, and internet packages are sold by the month. The big mobile networks include Zain, Asiacell and Korek. The shop usually asks for your ID to register a new line, and phone shops also repair screens and sell chargers and cases.

lessons.culture: Emergency numbers differ from country to country and the lines are not always the same everywhere in Iraq, so ask a local for the right number and save it in your phone before you need it. In Iraq the fire service is the civil defence (الدفاع المدني). When you call, say where you are first, speak slowly and stay on the line.

lessons.culture: After a road accident in Iraq the traffic police (شرطة المرور) usually come to write a report, and you normally keep your car where it is until they say otherwise unless it blocks the road. Ask for the report, since you need it for the insurance. Do not move anyone who is hurt, call for help, and ask a local for the right emergency number.

lessons.culture: In a crowded place such as a market or a busy shrine, go straight to a guard or to the information desk (الاستعلامات), who can announce it on the microphone and tell the others. Keep a recent photo of your child on your phone, and teach children early their father's name and your phone number. Stay calm so you can say the age, the clothes and the last place you saw him.

challenge.title: A morning of errands
challenge.instructions: Write and act out a conversation of at least 10 lines in Iraqi Arabic where you withdraw cash at the bank, ask where the post office is, ask the price of sending a parcel, and top up your phone balance. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 19, and use a polite word.
required_elements: a request at the bank with أريد أسحب
a question with وين about the post office or the shop
a question about a price with شكد
a request to top up with أشحن رصيدي
a polite word such as لو سمحت or مشكور
